items.body: Princeton Companions to Mathematics and Applied Mathematics is the answer. They include math history, overview of modern math domains, concepts, plenty of cross references (both within a book and in between applied and pure math), implications and interpretation of important math equations, laws, applications of math and so on and so forth. I’m surprised it was only mentioned in the comments once and not a heavily upvoted answer.

I loved The Calculus Gallery by William Dunham, which covers snapshots in the development of calculus: Newton, Leibniz, the Bernoullis, Cauchy, Riemann, Weierstrass, Baire, and Lebesgue. It's full of real maths — full-blown results and detailed proofs — but explained very clearly and easy to read. Accessible, enjoyable, fascinating, and educational!

I haven't looked at it very closely, but perhaps the Princeton Companion to Mathematics? It's more encyclopedic in nature, but I believe it's intended to be fairly accessible. It might be something to dip in and out of.

Not necessarily math but the book An Elementary Primer for Gauge Theory by K. Moriasu is a great read for anyone interested in Quantum Field Theory, mixing history, light hand-waving proofs/derivations, and physics. It's really short too. It's outdated now in light of more recent discoveries but still a great book.
Not a book, but the ICM surveys (impa.br/icm2018) are often great for getting a very basic idea of what's going on in various fields outside of one's own.
This describes history of mathematics rather than casual mathematics. For me "casual mathematics" would mean a causal, hand-waving, light-on-the-proof-details description of mathematical results.
I really enjoyed History of Topology by I.M. James. It's a very casual read, but walks you through a lot of "advanced" mathematics.
I really liked Love & Math by Edward Frenkel.
This is not history of mathematics, and I don't know if the material can be considered "advanced" in any sense but looks fun: bookstore.ams.org/mbk-46
These seem very interesting, thanks for the suggestion!

Dieudonne has a few maths history books on algebraic geometry and algebraic geometry, which explain the context in which these fields developed.  The Grothendieck-Serre correspondence contains an exchange of letters of who might be the most influential postwar mathematicians. Villani has his book "the birth of a theorem" or something like that.
